States, supports, stability and symmetry · Open Mathematics Courses

The Effros Borel structure

Self-checked by the writing AI. Original text: CC0 1.0.

A direct integral of von Neumann algebras is assembled from a family γ↦M(γ)\gamma\mapsto M(\gamma)γ↦M(γ) of von Neumann algebras that depends measurably on a parameter γ\gammaγ. To make sense of this, one needs a Borel structure on a set of von Neumann algebras, and workable tests for measurability. This lesson supplies both.

We give a Borel structure, the Effros Borel structure, to three sets: the weak*-closed subspaces of the dual of a separable Banach space, the closed subspaces of a separable Hilbert space, and the von Neumann algebras acting on a fixed separable Hilbert space. We show that these Borel spaces are standard, that their elements can be chosen in a Borel way, and that adjoints, commutants, intersections, joins and the set of factors are Borel. We then embed every measurable field of Hilbert spaces isometrically into one fixed space, with ranges that depend measurably on the point. With this we show that commutants, centres, intersections and joins of measurably generated families of von Neumann algebras are again measurably generated. These are the measurability facts that direct integrals of von Neumann algebras need.

Sections 1–5 need only basic functional analysis and metric topology. Sections 6, 7 and 10 use measurable fields of Hilbert spaces and of operators, as developed in Measurable fields of Hilbert spaces and their direct integrals, and a few facts from Decomposable operators and the diagonal algebra. Sections 8–10 use the predual of B(K)B(\mathcal K)B(K) and its σ\sigmaσ-weak topology. The facts used without proof are stated in full below. No measure is used anywhere: every result holds over an arbitrary measurable space.

Effros introduced the Borel space of von Neumann algebras on a separable Hilbert space in 1965 [Effros 1965]. Basic references are [Effros 1965] and [Takesaki I].

1. Borel spaces and Polish spaces

Definitions 1.1.

  • A Borel space consists of a set XXX and a σ\sigmaσ-algebra B\mathcal BB of subsets of XXX, whose members are called Borel sets. A subset Y⊆XY\subseteq XY⊆X carries the relative Borel structure {B∩Y:B∈B}\{B\cap Y:B\in\mathcal B\}{B∩Y:B∈B}.
  • A map f:X→Yf:X\to Yf:X→Y of Borel spaces is Borel if f−1(B)f^{-1}(B)f−1(B) is Borel for every Borel B⊆YB\subseteq YB⊆Y. A Borel isomorphism is a bijection fff such that fff and f−1f^{-1}f−1 are Borel.
  • σ(S)\sigma(\mathcal S)σ(S) is the σ\sigmaσ-algebra generated by a family S\mathcal SS of sets. For maps fi:X→Yif_i:X\to Y_ifi​:X→Yi​ into Borel spaces, σ(fi:i∈I)\sigma(f_i:i\in I)σ(fi​:i∈I) is the smallest σ\sigmaσ-algebra that makes every fif_ifi​ Borel. A family of Borel sets is generating if it generates B\mathcal BB, and separating if for any two distinct points some member contains one of them and not the other. XXX is countably generated or countably separated if it has a countable family of that kind. A stronger condition asks for a single countable family that both generates and separates. Proposition 3.2(5) supplies such a family, so its conclusion holds in either sense.
  • The Borel structure of a topological space is the σ\sigmaσ-algebra generated by its open sets.
  • A topological space is Polish when its topology comes from a complete metric and it has a countable dense subset. A Borel space is standard when some Polish space, with its Borel sets, is Borel isomorphic to it.
  • A measure on (X,B)(X,\mathcal B)(X,B) is a countably additive map μ:B→[0,∞]\mu:\mathcal B\to[0,\infty]μ:B→[0,∞]. It is standard if X∖NX\setminus NX∖N, with its relative Borel structure, is standard for some Borel set NNN with μ(N)=0\mu(N)=0μ(N)=0.

Example 1.2. A Borel map need not carry Borel sets to Borel sets. The identity map from R\mathbb RR with its Borel sets to R\mathbb RR with the σ\sigmaσ-algebra of countable and co-countable sets is Borel, since every set of the second kind is Borel. It carries the Borel set [0,1][0,1][0,1] to a set that is neither countable nor co-countable.

Lemma 1.3.

  1. (Testing on generators) Suppose B=σ(fi:i∈I)\mathcal B=\sigma(f_i:i\in I)B=σ(fi​:i∈I). A map g:Γ→Xg:\Gamma\to Xg:Γ→X is measurable if and only if every fi∘gf_i\circ gfi​∘g is measurable.
  2. (Countable bases) If a topological space has a countable base U\mathcal UU, every open set is a countable union of members of U\mathcal UU, so the Borel sets are σ(U)\sigma(\mathcal U)σ(U). The Borel structure of a product of countably many second countable spaces is generated by the coordinate maps. In particular, for a countable set DDD, the Borel structure of RD\mathbb R^DRD is generated by the coordinates.
  3. (A stock of Polish spaces) Closed subsets and countable products of Polish spaces are Polish, and so is the disjoint union of two Polish spaces, each piece open in the union. The space NN\mathbb N^{\mathbb N}NN is Polish. A separable metrizable space, and hence every standard Borel space, has at most 2ℵ02^{\aleph_0}2ℵ0​ points.
  4. (Pieces) Let Γ\GammaΓ be the union of countably many sets Γd∈Σ\Gamma_d\in\SigmaΓd​∈Σ. A map ggg on Γ\GammaΓ whose restriction to every Γd\Gamma_dΓd​ is measurable for the relative σ\sigmaσ-algebra is measurable.

(3) A closed subset of a complete metric space is complete, and a subset of a separable metric space is separable. For Polish spaces XkX_kXk​, choose complete compatible metrics dk≤1d_k\leq1dk​≤1 (replace dkd_kdk​ by min⁡(dk,1)\min(d_k,1)min(dk​,1)). Theorem 2.2 (Borel subsets of standard spaces). Let (X,τ)(X,\tau)(X,τ) be a Polish space and B⊆XB\subseteq XB⊆X a Borel set. There is a Polish topology τ′⊇τ\tau'\supseteq\tauτ′⊇τ on XXX, with the same Borel sets as τ\tauτ, in which BBB is open and closed. Consequently BBB, with its relative Borel structure, is a standard Borel space. The same holds for a Borel subset of any standard Borel space.

The proof uses only part (1) of Theorem 2.1.

Proof. Call a topology τ′\tau'τ′ on XXX admissible if it is Polish, contains τ\tauτ, and has the same Borel sets as τ\tauτ.

(a) Open sets. Let UUU be τ\tauτ-open, and let τU\tau_UτU​ be the topology generated by τ\tauτ together with the set X∖UX\setminus UX∖U. Its open sets are the unions of sets VVV and V∩(X∖U)V\cap(X\setminus U)V∩(X∖U) with V∈τV\in\tauV∈τ. So (X,τU)(X,\tau_U)(X,τU​) is the disjoint union of the open subspace UUU and the closed subspace X∖UX\setminus UX∖U of (X,τ)(X,\tau)(X,τ), each open in τU\tau_UτU​. Both pieces are Polish: UUU by Theorem 2.1(1), since an open set is a GδG_\deltaGδ​, and X∖UX\setminus UX∖U because closed subsets of Polish spaces are Polish (Lemma 1.3(3)). By the same lemma, their disjoint union is Polish. The new open sets are τ\tauτ-Borel. So τU\tau_UτU​ is admissible, and UUU is τU\tau_UτU​-clopen.

(b) Countable joins. Let τ1,τ2,…\tau_1,\tau_2,\ldotsτ1​,τ2​,… be admissible, and let τ∞\tau_\inftyτ∞​ be the topology generated by their union. The diagonal map x↦(x,x,…)x\mapsto(x,x,\ldots)x↦(x,x,…) from (X,τ∞)(X,\tau_\infty)(X,τ∞​) to the Polish space ∏n(X,τn)\prod_n(X,\tau_n)∏n​(X,τn​) is a homeomorphism onto the diagonal Δ\DeltaΔ, since the preimage of πn−1(V)\pi_n^{-1}(V)πn−1​(V) is VVV for V∈τnV\in\tau_nV∈τn​. The diagonal is closed: if y∉Δy\notin\Deltay∈/Δ, then ym≠yny_m\neq y_nym​=yn​ for some m,nm,nm,n; since τ\tauτ is Hausdorff, there are disjoint τ\tauτ-open sets A∋ymA\ni y_mA∋ym​ and C∋ynC\ni y_nC∋yn​, and πm−1(A)∩πn−1(C)\pi_m^{-1}(A)\cap\pi_n^{-1}(C)πm−1​(A)∩πn−1​(C) is a neighbourhood of yyy that misses Δ\DeltaΔ. So τ∞\tau_\inftyτ∞​ is Polish, because a closed subset of a Polish space is Polish. It has a countable base consisting of finite intersections of members of countable bases of the τn\tau_nτn​. These are τ\tauτ-Borel, and a countable base generates the Borel sets (Lemma 1.3(2)). So τ∞\tau_\inftyτ∞​ has the same Borel sets as τ\tauτ, and it is admissible.

(c) All Borel sets. Let A\mathcal AA be the family of sets that are clopen for some admissible topology. It contains τ\tauτ by (a), and it is closed under complements. If Bn∈AB_n\in\mathcal ABn​∈A is clopen for an admissible τn\tau_nτn​, then ⋃nBn\bigcup_nB_n⋃n​Bn​ is open for the τ∞\tau_\inftyτ∞​ of (b); applying (a) to (X,τ∞)(X,\tau_\infty)(X,τ∞​) makes it clopen for a topology that is admissible. So A\mathcal AA is a σ\sigmaσ-algebra containing τ\tauτ, and it contains every Borel set.

Now let BBB be clopen for an admissible τ′\tau'τ′. Then BBB is τ′\tau'τ′-closed, hence Polish in the relative τ′\tau'τ′-topology (Lemma 1.3(3)). The Borel sets of a subspace are the traces of the Borel sets of the whole space: the traces form a σ\sigmaσ-algebra on BBB containing the relatively open sets, and the sets CCC whose trace is Borel in BBB form a σ\sigmaσ-algebra containing the open sets. The τ′\tau'τ′-Borel sets are the τ\tauτ-Borel sets, so the relative Borel structure of BBB is the Borel structure of a Polish space. For a standard Borel space, transport BBB to a Polish space by a Borel isomorphism. □\square□

We now show that the Effros Borel structure is standard, by exhibiting a Polish topology that generates it.

Example 4.4 (separability cannot be dropped). Let vN(K)\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)vN(K) be the set of von Neumann algebras on K\mathcal KK, with the Borel structure induced from W(B(K))\mathfrak W(B(\mathcal K))W(B(K)).

Theorem 9.1.

  1. vN(K)={M∈W(B(K)):M∗=M and M′′=M}\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)=\{M\in\mathfrak W(B(\mathcal K)):M^*=M\text{ and }M''=M\}vN(K)={M∈W(B(K)):M∗=M and M′′=M}. It is a Borel subset of W(B(K))\mathfrak W(B(\mathcal K))W(B(K)), and a standard Borel space.
  2. (Borel choice of generators) There are Borel maps an:vN(K)→B(K)1a_n:\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)\to B(\mathcal K)_1an​:vN(K)→B(K)1​ with an(M)∈M1a_n(M)\in M_1an​(M)∈M1​ and {an(M):n}\{a_n(M):n\}{an​(M):n} σ\sigmaσ-weakly dense in M1M_1M1​. In particular MMM is generated by {an(M):n}\{a_n(M):n\}{an​(M):n}.
  3. (Measurability criterion) A map γ↦M(γ)∈vN(K)\gamma\mapsto M(\gamma)\in\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)γ↦M(γ)∈vN(K) is measurable if and only if there are weakly measurable maps ai:Γ→B(K)a_i:\Gamma\to B(\mathcal K)ai​:Γ→B(K), i≥1i\geq1i≥1, such that M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ) is generated by {ai(γ):i}\{a_i(\gamma):i\}{ai​(γ):i} for every γ\gammaγ. When MMM is measurable, the aia_iai​ can be chosen with values in B(K)1B(\mathcal K)_1B(K)1​ and σ\sigmaσ-weakly dense in M(γ)1M(\gamma)_1M(γ)1​.
  4. (Intersections, joins and commutants) The maps (M,N)↦M∩N(M,N)\mapsto M\cap N(M,N)↦M∩N and (M,N)↦M∨N(M,N)\mapsto M\vee N(M,N)↦M∨N are Borel from vN(K)×vN(K)\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)\times\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)vN(K)×vN(K) to vN(K)\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)vN(K), and M↦M′M\mapsto M'M↦M′ is a Borel map of vN(K)\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)vN(K) into itself.
  5. (Factors) The set of factors is a Borel subset of vN(K)\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)vN(K), and a standard Borel space.

Proof. (1) A von Neumann algebra is σ\sigmaσ-weakly closed (see the Conventions), self-adjoint, and equal to its bicommutant. Conversely, let M∈W(B(K))M\in\mathfrak W(B(\mathcal K))M∈W(B(K)) satisfy M∗=MM^*=MM∗=M and M′′=MM''=MM′′=M. A commutant is always a unital algebra, and the commutant of a self-adjoint set is self-adjoint. So M′M'M′ and M′′=MM''=MM′′=M are unital ∗*∗-algebras, and MMM is a von Neumann algebra. The maps M↦M∗M\mapsto M^*M↦M∗ and M↦M′′M\mapsto M''M↦M′′ are Borel by Theorem 8.2, and fixed-point sets of Borel maps are Borel (Proposition 3.2(6)); so the set is Borel. W(B(K))\mathfrak W(B(\mathcal K))W(B(K)) is standard by Theorem 4.1, and Borel subsets of standard Borel spaces are standard by Theorem 2.2.

(2) Restrict the maps of Theorem 5.3 to vN(K)\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)vN(K). The von Neumann algebra generated by {an(M)}\{a_n(M)\}{an​(M)} is σ\sigmaσ-weakly closed and contains the an(M)a_n(M)an​(M), hence M1M_1M1​ and MMM. It is contained in MMM, since MMM is a von Neumann algebra containing the an(M)a_n(M)an​(M).

(3) If MMM is measurable, the maps ai∘Ma_i\circ Mai​∘M, with aia_iai​ from (2), are measurable into B(K)1B(\mathcal K)_1B(K)1​, hence weakly measurable (Lemma 8.1(2)), and they generate M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ). Conversely, let S(γ)={ai(γ),ai(γ)∗:i}S(\gamma)=\{a_i(\gamma),a_i(\gamma)^*:i\}S(γ)={ai​(γ),ai​(γ)∗:i}, a countable family of weakly measurable maps (Lemma 8.1(2)). Then γ↦S(γ)′\gamma\mapsto S(\gamma)'γ↦S(γ)′ is measurable by Theorem 8.2(2), and γ↦S(γ)′′=M(γ)\gamma\mapsto S(\gamma)''=M(\gamma)γ↦S(γ)′′=M(γ) is measurable by Theorem 8.2(3).

(4) Let ana_nan​ be as in (2), and give vN(K)×vN(K)\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)\times\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)vN(K)×vN(K) the product σ\sigmaσ-algebra. The maps (M,N)↦ai(M)(M,N)\mapsto a_i(M)(M,N)↦ai​(M) and (M,N)↦aj(N)(M,N)\mapsto a_j(N)(M,N)↦aj​(N) are weakly measurable, and so are (M,N)↦ai(M′)(M,N)\mapsto a_i(M')(M,N)↦ai​(M′) and (M,N)↦aj(N′)(M,N)\mapsto a_j(N')(M,N)↦aj​(N′), because M↦M′M\mapsto M'M↦M′ is Borel (Theorem 8.2(3)) and maps vN(K)\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)vN(K) into itself. Now M∨N=((M∪N)′)′=(M′∩N′)′=({ai(M),aj(N):i,j}′)′,M∩N=(M′∪N′)′={ai(M′),aj(N′):i,j}′. M\vee N=\big((M\cup N)'\big)'=(M'\cap N')'=\big(\{a_i(M),a_j(N):i,j\}'\big)',\qquad M\cap N=(M'\cup N')'=\{a_i(M'),a_j(N'):i,j\}' . M∨N=((M∪N)′)′=(M′∩N′)′=({ai​(M),aj​(N):i,j}′)′,M∩N=(M′∪N′)′={ai​(M′),aj​(N′):i,j}′. The second formula and the inner commutant of the first are measurable by Theorem 8.2(2), and the outer commutant is measurable by Theorem 8.2(3). The last claim is Theorem 8.2(3), since the commutant of a von Neumann algebra is one.

(5) The set is {M:M∩M′=C1}\{M:M\cap M'=\mathbb C1\}{M:M∩M′=C1}. The map M↦M∩M′M\mapsto M\cap M'M↦M∩M′ is Borel by (4), as the composite of M↦(M,M′)M\mapsto(M,M')M↦(M,M′) with the intersection map, and {C1}\{\mathbb C1\}{C1} is a point. Points are Borel (Proposition 3.2(6)), so the set of factors is Borel, and it is standard by Theorem 2.2. □\square□

Remarks 9.2. (a) Part (3) needs no bound on the generators, and part (2) supplies generators in the unit ball. (b) The restriction of the topology τE\tau_EτE​ of Theorem 4.1, for E=B(K)∗E=B(\mathcal K)_*E=B(K)∗​, to vN(K)\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)vN(K) is known as the Effros–Maréchal topology. It is Polish when K\mathcal KK is separable; see [Ando–Haagerup–Winsløw, Section 2.4], which refers to Haagerup and Winsløw for the original definition. By Theorem 2.1(2) this makes vN(K)\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)vN(K) a GδG_\deltaGδ​ subset of (W(B(K)),τE)(\mathfrak W(B(\mathcal K)),\tau_E)(W(B(K)),τE​). This lesson does not use these facts.

Example 9.3 (von Neumann algebras on C2\mathbb C^2C2). 11. Exercises

Exercise 1 (lattice operations). Show that P↦1−PP\mapsto1-PP↦1−P is a homeomorphism of P(K)\mathcal P(\mathcal K)P(K), that (P,Q)↦P∨Q(P,Q)\mapsto P\vee Q(P,Q)↦P∨Q and (P,Q)↦P∧Q(P,Q)\mapsto P\wedge Q(P,Q)↦P∧Q (the projections onto the closed span of PK+QKP\mathcal K+Q\mathcal KPK+QK and onto PK∩QKP\mathcal K\cap Q\mathcal KPK∩QK) are Borel maps P(K)×P(K)→P(K)\mathcal P(\mathcal K)\times\mathcal P(\mathcal K)\to\mathcal P(\mathcal K)P(K)×P(K)→P(K), and that {(P,Q):P≤Q}\{(P,Q):P\leq Q\}{(P,Q):P≤Q} is closed.

Solution. ⟨(1−P)ξ,η⟩=⟨ξ,η⟩−⟨Pξ,η⟩\langle(1-P)\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle\xi,\eta\rangle-\langle P\xi,\eta\rangle⟨(1−P)ξ,η⟩=⟨ξ,η⟩−⟨Pξ,η⟩, so P↦1−PP\mapsto1-PP↦1−P is weakly continuous, and it is its own inverse. On P(K)×P(K)\mathcal P(\mathcal K)\times\mathcal P(\mathcal K)P(K)×P(K) with the product σ\sigmaσ-algebra, the maps (P,Q)↦Pζn(P,Q)\mapsto P\zeta_n(P,Q)↦Pζn​ and (P,Q)↦Qζn(P,Q)\mapsto Q\zeta_n(P,Q)↦Qζn​, for a dense sequence (ζn)(\zeta_n)(ζn​), are measurable (Theorem 6.1(2)), and together they span a dense subspace of PK+QKP\mathcal K+Q\mathcal KPK+QK. So P∨QP\vee QP∨Q is Borel by criterion (c) of Theorem 6.1(3). Since PK∩QKP\mathcal K\cap Q\mathcal KPK∩QK is the orthogonal complement of (1−P)K+(1−Q)K(1-P)\mathcal K+(1-Q)\mathcal K(1−P)K+(1−Q)K, P∧Q=1−((1−P)∨(1−Q))P\wedge Q=1-\big((1-P)\vee(1-Q)\big)P∧Q=1−((1−P)∨(1−Q)), which is Borel. Finally, P≤QP\leq QP≤Q means PK⊆QKP\mathcal K\subseteq Q\mathcal KPK⊆QK. This holds exactly when ∥Pξ∥≤∥Qξ∥\|P\xi\|\leq\|Q\xi\|∥Pξ∥≤∥Qξ∥ for all ξ\xiξ. If PK⊆QKP\mathcal K\subseteq Q\mathcal KPK⊆QK, then P=PQP=PQP=PQ, so ∥Pξ∥=∥PQξ∥≤∥Qξ∥\|P\xi\|=\|PQ\xi\|\leq\|Q\xi\|∥Pξ∥=∥PQξ∥≤∥Qξ∥. Conversely, let ξ∈PK\xi\in P\mathcal Kξ∈PK and apply the inequality to (1−Q)ξ(1-Q)\xi(1−Q)ξ: P(1−Q)ξ=0P(1-Q)\xi=0P(1−Q)ξ=0, so ∥(1−Q)ξ∥2=⟨(1−Q)ξ,Pξ⟩=⟨P(1−Q)ξ,ξ⟩=0\|(1-Q)\xi\|^2=\langle(1-Q)\xi,P\xi\rangle=\langle P(1-Q)\xi,\xi\rangle=0∥(1−Q)ξ∥2=⟨(1−Q)ξ,Pξ⟩=⟨P(1−Q)ξ,ξ⟩=0, and ξ∈QK\xi\in Q\mathcal Kξ∈QK. Each condition ∥Pξ∥≤∥Qξ∥\|P\xi\|\leq\|Q\xi\|∥Pξ∥≤∥Qξ∥ is closed for the strong operator topology.

Exercise 2 (rank). Show that P↦dim⁡PK∈{0,1,…,∞}P\mapsto\dim P\mathcal K\in\{0,1,\ldots,\infty\}P↦dimPK∈{0,1,…,∞} is lower semicontinuous on P(K)\mathcal P(\mathcal K)P(K) with the strong operator topology, so that every set {P:dim⁡PK=r}\{P:\dim P\mathcal K=r\}{P:dimPK=r} is Borel. Show that it is continuous if dim⁡K<∞\dim\mathcal K<\inftydimK<∞, and not if dim⁡K=∞\dim\mathcal K=\inftydimK=∞.

Solution. Suppose dim⁡PK≥r\dim P\mathcal K\geq rdimPK≥r, with rrr finite, and choose orthonormal u1,…,ur∈PKu_1,\ldots,u_r\in P\mathcal Ku1​,…,ur​∈PK. If Q→PQ\to PQ→P strongly, then Qui→Pui=uiQu_i\to Pu_i=u_iQui​→Pui​=ui​. So the Gram matrix (⟨Qui,Quj⟩)(\langle Qu_i,Qu_j\rangle)(⟨Qui​,Quj​⟩) tends to the identity and is eventually invertible. Then Qu1,…,QurQu_1,\ldots,Qu_rQu1​,…,Qur​ are linearly independent, and dim⁡QK≥r\dim Q\mathcal K\geq rdimQK≥r. So {dim⁡≥r}\{\dim\geq r\}{dim≥r} is open for each finite rrr, and {dim⁡=r}={dim⁡≥r}∖{dim⁡≥r+1}\{\dim=r\}=\{\dim\geq r\}\setminus\{\dim\geq r+1\}{dim=r}={dim≥r}∖{dim≥r+1} and {dim⁡=∞}=⋂r{dim⁡≥r}\{\dim=\infty\}=\bigcap_r\{\dim\geq r\}{dim=∞}=⋂r​{dim≥r} are Borel. If dim⁡K<∞\dim\mathcal K<\inftydimK<∞, then dim⁡PK=tr⁡P=∑k⟨Pεk,εk⟩\dim P\mathcal K=\operatorname{tr}P=\sum_k\langle P\varepsilon_k,\varepsilon_k\rangledimPK=trP=∑k​⟨Pεk​,εk​⟩ is continuous. If dim⁡K=∞\dim\mathcal K=\inftydimK=∞, Example 6.3 gives rank-one projections converging to 000. For a map γ↦K(γ)\gamma\mapsto K(\gamma)γ↦K(γ) as in Theorem 6.1(3), composing with the rank recovers the measurability of γ↦dim⁡K(γ)\gamma\mapsto\dim K(\gamma)γ↦dimK(γ), which Theorem 6.1(3) obtained from the theory of subspace fields.

Exercise 3 (abelian algebras and inclusions). Show that the sets {M∈vN(K):M is abelian}\{M\in\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K):M\text{ is abelian}\}{M∈vN(K):M is abelian} and {M:M′=M}\{M:M'=M\}{M:M′=M} (the maximal abelian algebras), and the relation {(M,N):M⊆N}\{(M,N):M\subseteq N\}{(M,N):M⊆N}, are Borel.

Solution. MMM is abelian exactly when M⊆M′M\subseteq M'M⊆M′, that is, when M∩M′=MM\cap M'=MM∩M′=M. Similarly, M⊆NM\subseteq NM⊆N exactly when M∩N=MM\cap N=MM∩N=M. The maps involved are Borel by Theorem 9.1(4), and a set where two Borel maps into vN(K)\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)vN(K) agree is Borel by Proposition 3.2(6). The same applies to M′=MM'=MM′=M.

Exercise 4 (unitary conjugation). Let U(K)\mathcal U(\mathcal K)U(K) be the unitary group with the Borel sets of the strong operator topology. Show that (u,M)↦uMu∗(u,M)\mapsto uMu^*(u,M)↦uMu∗ is a Borel map U(K)×vN(K)→vN(K)\mathcal U(\mathcal K)\times\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)\to\mathrm{vN}(\mathcal K)U(K)×vN(K)→vN(K).

Solution. On the product, the maps (u,M)↦u(u,M)\mapsto u(u,M)↦u, (u,M)↦u∗(u,M)\mapsto u^*(u,M)↦u∗ and (u,M)↦an(M)(u,M)\mapsto a_n(M)(u,M)↦an​(M) (from Theorem 9.1(2)) are weakly measurable: ⟨uξ,η⟩\langle u\xi,\eta\rangle⟨uξ,η⟩ is continuous in uuu, and ⟨u∗ξ,η⟩\langle u^*\xi,\eta\rangle⟨u∗ξ,η⟩ is the conjugate of ⟨uη,ξ⟩\langle u\eta,\xi\rangle⟨uη,ξ⟩. Products of weakly measurable maps are weakly measurable (Lemma 8.1(2)), so the maps (u,M)↦uan(M)u∗(u,M)\mapsto ua_n(M)u^*(u,M)↦uan​(M)u∗ are weakly measurable. uMu∗uMu^*uMu∗ is generated by {uan(M)u∗}\{ua_n(M)u^*\}{uan​(M)u∗}, because x↦uxu∗x\mapsto uxu^*x↦uxu∗ is a ∗*∗-automorphism of B(K)B(\mathcal K)B(K) that carries commutants to commutants. Theorem 9.1(3) finishes the proof.

Exercise 5 (reduced algebras). Let (M(γ))(M(\gamma))(M(γ)) be a measurably generated family over a measurable field (H(γ)),M(H(\gamma)),\mathfrak M(H(γ)),M, and let ppp be a measurable field of projections with p(γ)∈M(γ)p(\gamma)\in M(\gamma)p(γ)∈M(γ) for every γ\gammaγ. Show that the subspaces p(γ)H(γ)p(\gamma)H(\gamma)p(γ)H(γ) form a measurable field, and that the reduced algebras p(γ)M(γ)p(γ)p(\gamma)M(\gamma)p(\gamma)p(γ)M(γ)p(γ), acting on p(γ)H(γ)p(\gamma)H(\gamma)p(γ)H(γ), form a measurably generated family. Show also that compressing an arbitrary generating set does not work.

Solution. The sections pekpe_kpek​ are measurable, by the definition of a measurable operator field, and they span a dense subspace of p(γ)H(γ)p(\gamma)H(\gamma)p(γ)H(γ) at each point. So the construction of subspace fields gives a measurable field (p(γ)H(γ))(p(\gamma)H(\gamma))(p(γ)H(γ)), whose measurable sections are the elements of M\mathfrak MM with values in p(γ)H(γ)p(\gamma)H(\gamma)p(γ)H(γ). By Theorem 10.3(2), choose measurable fields xnx_nxn​ with {xn(γ)}\{x_n(\gamma)\}{xn​(γ)} σ\sigmaσ-weakly dense in the unit ball of M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ). The fields pxnppx_nppxn​p are measurable, since composites of measurable operator fields are measurable, and they carry measurable sections of the subfield to elements of M\mathfrak MM with values in p(γ)H(γ)p(\gamma)H(\gamma)p(γ)H(γ); so they are measurable fields on the subfield. The reduced algebra p(γ)M(γ)p(γ)p(\gamma)M(\gamma)p(\gamma)p(γ)M(γ)p(γ) is a von Neumann algebra acting on p(γ)H(γ)p(\gamma)H(\gamma)p(γ)H(γ), by fact (R) of the background. The map x↦p(γ)xp(γ)x\mapsto p(\gamma)xp(\gamma)x↦p(γ)xp(γ) is σ\sigmaσ-weakly continuous and carries the unit ball of M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ) onto that of p(γ)M(γ)p(γ)p(\gamma)M(\gamma)p(\gamma)p(γ)M(γ)p(γ), because pxp=xpxp=xpxp=x for xxx in the reduced algebra. So the p(γ)xn(γ)p(γ)p(\gamma)x_n(\gamma)p(\gamma)p(γ)xn​(γ)p(γ) are σ\sigmaσ-weakly dense in that unit ball, and they generate it. For the warning: in M3(C)M_3(\mathbb C)M3​(C), the matrix units e11,e13,e32e_{11},e_{13},e_{32}e11​,e13​,e32​ generate M3(C)M_3(\mathbb C)M3​(C) (with their adjoints they give e12=e13e32e_{12}=e_{13}e_{32}e12​=e13​e32​, e21=e23e31e_{21}=e_{23}e_{31}e21​=e23​e31​, e33=e31e13e_{33}=e_{31}e_{13}e33​=e31​e13​, e22=e23e32e_{22}=e_{23}e_{32}e22​=e23​e32​, and so every matrix unit). The projection p=e11+e22p=e_{11}+e_{22}p=e11​+e22​ lies in M3(C)M_3(\mathbb C)M3​(C), but pe11p=e11pe_{11}p=e_{11}pe11​p=e11​, pe13p=0pe_{13}p=0pe13​p=0 and pe32p=0pe_{32}p=0pe32​p=0 generate only the diagonal algebra on pC3p\mathbb C^3pC3, while pM3(C)p≅M2(C)pM_3(\mathbb C)p\cong M_2(\mathbb C)pM3​(C)p≅M2​(C). This is why the solution uses the generators of Theorem 10.3(2), which are dense in the unit ball.

Where this leads

  • Polish spaces and standard Borel spaces continues the descriptive set theory of Sections 1, 2 and 4: Souslin spaces, the isomorphism theorem for standard Borel spaces, and measurable cross sections.
  • Direct integrals of von Neumann algebras: over a measure space, a measurably generated family (M(γ))(M(\gamma))(M(γ)) defines the von Neumann algebra ∫⊕M(γ) dμ(γ)\int^\oplus M(\gamma)\,d\mu(\gamma)∫⊕M(γ)dμ(γ) of decomposable operators whose fibres lie in the M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ). Theorem 10.3 supplies the measurability facts behind its commutant and its centre: the families of commutants and of centres are again measurably generated, and the set of points where the fibre is a factor is measurable.
